abstract: Regulation of motor variability is a key hallmark of motor skill learning, balancing motor exploration with optimization of identified task solutions. Nevertheless, the underlying circuit mechanisms in the mammalian brain remain largely unknown. Subnuclei of the dorsal striatum in the basal ganglia promote stereotyped or variable behavior, respectively, and deep brain stimulation of the downstream subthalamic nucleus (STN) can alter motor variability. We therefore tested whether the STN regulates motor variability via non-canonical projections to striatum. We discovered that silencing STN neurons projecting to dorsolateral striatum impaired motor variability reduction in rats developing complex stereotyped movement patterns. In contrast, silencing STN neurons projecting to the anterior thalamic nuclei, or neurons in these nuclei that receive STN input and project to dorsomedial striatum, accelerated variability reduction. These results deepen our anatomical and functional understanding of subcortical motor circuits and reveal unknown roles for STN's non-canonical striatal projections in motor variability regulation.
